Imagine being able to erase, from all human minds and records, what has happened in the past. An individual whom I respect and admire was discussing this question, and I was very surprised to hear that they would indeed push the button. He argued that painlessly and seamlessly removing it would get rid of feuds and prejudices, as well as long-standing traditions that no longer have place in society. In this scenario, we retain scientific knowledge - calculus is here, but Isaac Newton is unknown. Political theories are available - we know of communism and the various electoral systems, but Marx, Stalin, Socrates and Voltaire are unknown. Cars but no Ford, Apple but no Steve Jobs, et cetera. Would you push the button or pass?
If you could erase all of history at the push of a button, would you?

Perhaps its more optimistic than realistic, but I believe that the baggage of history isn't eternal. I believe that humans can collectively phase out the ill effects without losing the rich history we have, and therefore I wouldn't push the button to erase all of history.

I would think that without the context of how these things arose, just having them is less worthwhile. Nuclear weapons without the anguished history of their use? Forgetting the bad is exactly what we ought to avoid. Acceptance and forgiveness are far worthier aspirations to my mind.

Hmmm. I am having a tough time wrapping my head around the idea that we could understand the concepts and sciences of the universe without knowing who gifted our understanding of them to society. I mean, obviously gravity exists. And it has existed for as far back in time as we know. But it was Sir Isaac Newton who allowed us to understand what it was. So, are we saying that people such as Newton have influenced us, but we don't know who has influenced us, or how? I am having a hard time comprehending how that would work, and I actually think it would be a lot more interesting to entertain the idea of wiping out our history and starting over. Rebooting our universe, so to speak.

In tackling that idea, though, I would really have to consider it as "rebooting our species." The reason I would have to look at it this way is because I have always felt that the Big Bang theory lacks merit and will eventually be proven as false. Don't get me wrong. Natural theology is even more absurd. There may not be a lot of evidence to support the theory of Gravity's Rainbow right now. But it's a relatively new idea, and I think that in the future, it will prove to be very credible, as it satisfies a lot of the problems that scientists have had with intelligent design, as well as the problems that religious persons have had with cosmological explanations. It's the best of both worlds. The fact that rainbow gravity would imply no beginning to the universe, however, reasons that it would be impossible to reboot our universe back to the beginning (because there is no beginning).

So, with that being said, would I choose to reboot our species? I don't think so. We have come quite a long way, and I think it would be interesting to see how this plays out. Society will eventually phase out any flaws in the system. It just takes time. If we were to start over, all we would be doing is erasing the progress that we have made. We would be back to square-one, and that doesn't help anybody. We wouldn't be starting over as a utopia. We would be starting over with all of mankind's flaws still intact, but without the understanding of our flaws and the ability to overcome them.
